en: Translated by Imperial Decree by Song Guṇabhadra;
annotated together by Imperial Decree by the Subject Monk Zongle, Abbot of the Chan Temple Shanshi Tianjie,
and the Subject Monk Ruxi, Abbot of the Lecture Hall Temple Yanfu.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I pray that the World-Honored One will further explain for me the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas). Since there is no self therein, who is it that arises and who is it that ceases?”
"Fools rely upon arising and ceasing; they do not awaken to the exhaustion of suffering, nor do they recognize nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"Listen attentively!
I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"Indeed, we shall receive your instructions.

Although the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) were already explained in the preceding text, Mahāmati again makes this request with the underlying intention that, regarding the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, there is both delusion and liberation; through liberation, those phenomena are devoid of self, so who is it that undergoes arising and ceasing?
Because they are deluded, fools rely upon birth and death; if their lack of awakening were exhausted, they would not recognize *nirvāṇa*. How, then, could they escape from birth and death?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The Tathāgata-garbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, capable of universally producing all realms of existence."

For example, it is like an actor who manifests various states of existence; being devoid of "self" and "what belongs to self," these states arise through the skillful means of the conjunction of three conditions.
Because externalists do not perceive this, they falsely cling to a creator. Perfumed by beginningless, false, and evil habits, this is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).
The ground of the abiding of ignorance arises together with the seven consciousnesses; like the body of ocean waves, it is constantly produced without interruption.
It is free from the fault of impermanence and free from the discourse of self; its intrinsic nature is stainless and ultimately pure.

Regarding the response which states that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome: "Tathāgata" refers to the Tathāgata as the principle-nature (*li-xing*); that which is possessed within the single thought-moment of the present is termed the "garbha" (womb/store).

When the faculties, objects, and the single thought-moment arise together, they follow along with conditions that are either defiled or pure. Defilement is ignorance; following the defiled conditions of ignorance, one undergoes the cycle of birth and death within the nine realms.
Purity is the teachings and practice; following the pure conditions of the teachings and practice, one attains the fourfold cessation of the path.
The four kinds are namely arising-and-ceasing, non-arising, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned; therefore it is said, "These are the causes of the good and the not-good.
Since causes evoke fruits, the phrase "all realms of rebirth" refers to the karmic retributions of good and evil within the ten realms.

For example, the lower illustrates the upper: the dharmas created according to conditions are fundamentally free from the two selves. It is like an actor who, by relying on incantations and arts, manifests various forms and images; how could there be any clinging to the two selves?
What are the three conditions?

They are the sense organs, the objects, and consciousness. When the sense organs and objects harmonize, a single thought-moment arises; because of non-awakening, it pursues defiled conditions, creating only delusion and karma, thereby forming the cycle of birth and death within the nine realms.

Because those non-Buddhists lack awakening, they engage in false conceptualization and attachment through mental construction; permeated by beginningless evil habits, this is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).
From it, the seven evolving consciousnesses arise, which abide in the ground of namelessness.

To speak of ignorance (*avidyā*) is to refer to the beginning of its arising; from this root, the derivative branches of ignorance are produced. Therefore, it is metaphorically described as "the body of ocean waves constantly arising without interruption."
This describes how, following defiled conditions, one proceeds from the subtle to the coarse.

If one can, in a single thought-moment, turn the light back within and accord with pure conditions, then one will be free from the fault of impermanence and the grasping at the two selves; the self-nature will be intrinsically pure, and what is called the Tathāgata of inherent virtue will be fully revealed.
"The remaining consciousnesses undergo arising and ceasing; within the mental faculty and the mental consciousness, there are seven [consciousnesses] at every moment.

Due to unreal conceptualization (*parikalpita-vikalpa*), they grasp at various objects, calculating and clinging to names and characteristics (*nāma-rūpa*) according to their diverse forms and locations. Failing to realize that these manifested forms and appearances are projections of one's own mind, and failing to perceive suffering and pleasure as they truly are, they do not attain liberation."
Regarding names, signs, and the various fetters, craving arises and produces further craving, whether as its cause or its object of apprehension.

When those faculties of sensation cease and do not arise in succession, one is no longer aware of pleasure or pain through the false imaginings of one's own mind; thus one enters the fourth meditative attainment, the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
This statement indicates that all consciousnesses undergo arising and ceasing.

"All consciousnesses" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the manas-consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*), and the five sensory consciousnesses; these constitute the seven consciousnesses, not the seventh consciousness of the followers of the Two Vehicles.
Arising from moment to moment, these arisings must be simultaneous.
Regarding the phrase "due to unreal conceptualization," this refers to the six consciousnesses apprehending their objects.

"Various forms and locations" refers to the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); once the faculties and their objects have taken form, they subsequently give rise to names and characteristics (*nāmanimitta*).

Because one does not understand that forms and other phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to feelings of suffering and pleasure, transmigrating through birth and death without means for liberation.
Bound by names and signs, greed arises from greed; cause and object mutually depend upon one another—all of which are what is called the characteristic of arising.

The subsiding of those various sensations is called the characteristic of cessation; that is to say, the faculties of sensation, as well as perception, mental formations, and so forth, arise no longer in succession, leaving only the deluded imaginings of one's own mind, wherein suffering and pleasure are no longer perceived.

To speak of "entering the cessation of feeling and perception" means that feeling, perception, and the mind have ceased; this refers either to the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) or to the attainment of the fourth dhyāna.
"A practitioner who skillfully understands the truths and practices liberation conceives the notion of liberation."
That which is neither separated from nor transformed is called the *tathāgatagarbha-vijñāna*; the seven consciousnesses flow on without ceasing.
Why is this so? Because those [seven] consciousnesses arise by taking that [garbha] as their causal object.

This is not the sphere of practice for Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; they do not realize non-self and, through the grasping of self-characteristics and common characteristics, give rise to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Upon seeing the Tathāgatagarbha, the five dharmas, the three natures, and the non-self of persons and phenomena are extinguished.

"Good, true reality, liberation," and so forth, refer to what is cultivated by the śrāvakas; they conceive of this meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) as liberation, yet it is not ultimate cessation.
Regarding "not departing" and "not revolving," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"In reality, one has not yet relinquished or transformed the name 'store-consciousness' (*ālayavijñāna*) within the Tathāgatagarbha; if there were no store-consciousness, the seven consciousnesses would cease."
Because they neither transform nor cease, the seven consciousnesses arise with the sixth consciousness as their cause and object of perception (*ālambana*).

However, this is not the sphere of experience known by practitioners of the Two Vehicles, for they only realize the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), grasping at the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

If one perceives the Tathāgatagarbha, then the five dharmas and the three natures are all devoid of the characteristic of self; how could the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases not be extinguished?
"The stages proceed in succession, advancing step by step."

Other heterodox views cannot shake or move him; this is called abiding in the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), wherein he attains the bliss of the thirteen gates to the path of samādhi.

Sustained by the awakening of samādhi, he contemplates the inconceivable Buddha-dharma. By his own vow, he does not accept the bliss of the gates to samādhi nor the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), but turns toward the noble realization of self-awakening—a path not shared with any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or heterodox practitioners.

One attains the path of the ten noble lineages (*āryagotra*) and the body born of mind through gnosis (*jñānamanomaya-kāya*), becoming free from the practice of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Therefore, Mahāmati,
a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who desires to seek supreme progress should purify the Tathāgatagarbha and that which is named the Ālayavijñāna.

"By virtue of the aforementioned realization, one attains entry into the first bhūmi; progressing through the stages in succession, with one's position deepened and virtues manifest, one is no longer moved by the false views of non-Buddhists, reaching the eighth Immovable Bhūmi."
In this state, one attains ten kinds of gateways to the bliss of samādhi and is sustained by the power of the samādhis of all Buddhas.
Awakening is itself Buddhahood.

One is then able to contemplate the dharmas of all Buddhas and the power of their original vows; unlike those of the Hīnayāna who cling to the bliss of samādhi or fail to abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one thus gives rise to transformative manifestations to benefit sentient beings.
Having attained the wisdom of self-realization, how could it be the same as the practices of ordinary beings or those of the Lesser Vehicle?
One who attains the path of the ten noble saintly natures (āryagotra) is one who possesses the saintly nature of the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
The ten stages are all "sages" (ārya); the inclusion of the term "worthy ones" (bhadra) is said in relation to the ultimate positions.

Regarding the phrase "the body, wisdom, and the mind-born," this refers to the progression from the ten stages up to the Buddha-stage: the body is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), wisdom is the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya), and the mind-born is the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).
Having attained the three bodies and being free from the causal practices of samādhi, the exhortation regarding the precepts states:
"Those who wish to advance further and reach the stage of a Tathāgata should purify the name of the Tathāgata’s ālayavijñāna."
The Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally without anything to be purified; it is merely its defilements that are cleansed.

As for designating the "consciousness-store" (vijñānagarbha) by means of names and words, this arises because one is deluded regarding the Tathāgatagarbha and it transforms into false consciousness; since it has no separate essence, it possesses only a name.
If there were no name for the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), then the transformation of the deluded consciousness would be the Tathāgatagarbha. "Mahāmati!
If the storehouse-consciousness did not exist under the name of Tathāgatagarbha, then there would be neither arising nor ceasing."
Mahāmati!

Nevertheless, all ordinary beings and noble ones alike possess birth and cessation; yet the practitioner, through the noble realization of self-awareness, dwells in the bliss of the present dharma without abandoning skillful means.
Mahāmati!

This Tathāgata-garbha, which is the ālayavijñāna, is seen by the mental conceptions of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as being pure in its own nature; yet, because it is covered by adventitious defilements, they perceive it as impure, whereas this is not the case for the Tathāgatas.
"Mahāmati!
The Tathāgata is one whose objective realm is directly manifest, like looking at an āmalaka fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
Since the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, now that it has returned to its original state, how could there be any arising or ceasing?"
Now, as for the fact that both ordinary beings and sages all possess birth and cessation: "ordinary beings" refers to external ordinary beings and internal ordinary beings.
External ordinary beings are those in the ten stages of faith;
internal ordinary beings are those in the stages of abiding, practice, and orientation, who are also called "the worthy."
The "sages" refer to those of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Although these sages possess birth and cessation—meaning that while they are able to practice and attain the noble realization of self-awakening—they still abide in the state of a cause and have not yet transcended the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "not abandoning skillful means": first, there are the skillful means for increasing the Path through one's own practice; second, there are the skillful means for benefiting others through transformation. Both possess the significance of arising and ceasing.
Regarding this Tathāgatagarbha and so forth, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"This Tathāgatagarbha, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), is pure by nature; it becomes impure when defiled by adventitious stains."
All those of the two vehicles and the various non-Buddhists give rise to views through mere conjecture and cannot realize this through direct perception.
The Tathāgata, however, perceives it clearly and directly, as if looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand.

“Mahāmati! By means of my supernormal power, I have established this principle so that Queen Śrīmālā and those bodhisattvas who are perfected in sharp intelligence may proclaim and expound upon the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna, [explaining] that the seven consciousnesses arise simultaneously, and how śrāvakas are attached to their views regarding the non-self of persons and phenomena.”

Therefore, Lady Śrīmālā, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, has expounded the realm of the Tathāgata, which is not the realm of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths.

The Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna are the sphere of wisdom accessible only to Buddhas and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of sharp faculties who rely upon the meaning; for this reason, you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently practice and study the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna, and do not merely be satisfied with hearing and understanding them.
Below this, I shall cite the sūtras spoken in the past as proof.
Although the Tathāgata’s teachings do not require external proof, they have already been explained extensively in those sūtras; therefore, by speaking briefly here, I am able to refer back to them.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:

"I, together with Queen Śrīmālā and other bodhisattvas of profound, wondrous, and pure wisdom, speak of the Tathāgatagarbha as the 'consciousness-store' (*vijñānagarbha*), which arises simultaneously with the seven consciousnesses, so that all śrāvakas may perceive the selflessness of phenomena."
Thus, the passage following the section on Śrīmālā is clearly evident.

Regarding the statement, "Do not merely hear or perceive [this] and conceive the thought that you have attained sufficient knowledge," it means that the Tathāgatagarbha and Ālayavijñāna are the realm of the Buddhas; those who do not possess the three types of wisdom cannot reach them. This is precisely where the exhortation to cultivate and study lies.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The profound Tathāgatagarbha Coexists with the seven consciousnesses;
Born from two kinds of grasping, The wise one remains far removed from it."
As reflections appear in a mirror, so the mind is perfumed by beginningless habitual tendencies;
for one who observes according to reality, all phenomena are found to be without intrinsic reality.
Like a fool who, seeing the finger pointing at the moon, looks at the finger and not at the moon.
Those who are attached to names and words do not see my true reality.
The mind is like an actor, the intellect is like the stage manager,
the five consciousnesses are its companions, and false discrimination is the audience watching the performance.

The verse above states that the Tathāgatagarbha coexists with the seven consciousnesses; furthermore, through the grasping of both specific and general characteristics, the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) arise—this refers to those who follow delusive conditions.
If one can reverse false views and realize the Tathāgatagarbha, then one will be far removed from birth and death.

The analogies such as reflections in a mirror were explained above; they mean that the essential nature of the eight consciousnesses is originally devoid of substantiality, yet due to being perfumed by beginningless evil habits, the various consciousnesses and their phenomena arise in transformation, just as images appear in a mirror.
When one contemplates in accordance with the nature of reality, images vanish like empty phenomena.

Furthermore, using the finger pointing at the moon as a metaphor for provisional names and substantial dharmas—whether there is gain or loss—if one cannot forget the words to accord with the principle, it is precisely like looking at the finger instead of the moon.
The "mind" (citta) refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind, which undergoes transformation according to conditions, like a performer manifesting illusions.

The "intellect" (manas) is the faculty of mind (*manendriya*), which further gives rise to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); this consciousness produces good and evil, like a musician who accompanies the performance.
The five consciousnesses grasp objects while the mental consciousness arises simultaneously with them; these constitute their companions.
Conceptual discrimination is like watching a theatrical performance.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain for us the ultimate analytical characteristics of the five dharmas, the self-natures, the consciousnesses, and the two kinds of non-self.
By means of this, I and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may, throughout all stages in continuous succession, analyze these dharmas and enter into all Buddha-dharmas.”
"Entering into all Buddha-dharmas extends even to the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very well, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“The characteristics of the five dharmas, the self-natures, the consciousnesses, and the two kinds of non-self, which constitute the various modes of differentiation, are namely: name, appearance, conceptualization, correct knowledge, and suchness.”

If a practitioner cultivates the entry into the Tathāgata’s personally realized noble path, they become free from views such as annihilationism, eternalism, existence, and non-existence, and the dwelling in the meditative attainment of happiness in the present life manifests before them.
Mahāmati!

Failing to realize those five dharmas, the self-natures, consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness—namely, that external objects are manifestations of one's own mind—is the deluded imagination of ordinary people, not that of the noble sages.

Although the five dharmas and so forth have already been clarified above, they have never yet been analyzed according to the various stages (*bhūmi*) to demonstrate how one enters all Buddha-dharmas and reaches the stage of a Tathāgata; therefore, he requests this once again.

In the response, the characteristics of delusion and awakening regarding the five dharmas are first presented in general. That is to say, when a practitioner enters [the path], these five dharmas are all characteristics of awakening; therefore, it says, "If a practitioner," and so forth.
If one reverses this, it is non-awakening; thus, these five dharmas are collectively delusive characteristics. Therefore, it is said that "one does not awaken to those five dharmas," and so forth.
One thereby knows that dharmas have no self-nature, and that delusion or awakening depends on the person.
This is merely a general indication; the specific characteristics of how one enters [the path] and so forth are fully detailed in the subsequent text.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
"How is it that false conceptualization arises in fools, but not in the noble ones?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Fools are attached to conventional names and signs; they follow after them as their minds flow and scatter."
Once they have dispersed, they fall into views of "I" and "mine" through various appearances and forms, and they long for and become attached to exquisite colors.
Having become attached, they are shrouded by ignorance, and thus give rise to defiled clinging.
Once stained by attachment, karma born of greed, hatred, and delusion is accumulated.

Having been accumulated, one entangles oneself with false imaginings like a silkworm spinning its cocoon, falling into the ocean of birth and death and the wilderness of the various realms of existence, like the wheel of a water-drawing well.

Due to ignorance, they are unable to know that the self-nature of things is like a magical illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water—devoid of "I" and "mine"—and thus give rise to all manner of unreal conceptualizations.

The characteristic, the characterized, and arising, abiding, and ceasing arise from the false imaginings of one's own mind; they do not arise from Īśvara, time, atoms, or primordial matter (pradhāna).

"Deluded ordinary beings fall; they flow with names and signs. In this analysis and explanation, the text specifically addresses delusive discrimination regarding names and signs to demonstrate the nature of confusion within the dharmas of ordinary beings. That is to say, based on the conventional designations of names and signs such as the six sense objects, they give rise to various discriminations. Their minds scatter and wander in delusion, falling into the views of "self" and "what belongs to self," and harboring expectations and attachments toward form. This obscures noble wisdom, giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, and leading them to perform various karmic actions. Like a silkworm spinning its cocoon, they entangle themselves with their own delusive thoughts, falling into the great ocean of birth and death across the various realms of existence.
The above descriptions of deluded states show that there is no escape from the three realms; this is clearly evident in the text.
The simile of the silkworm spinning its cocoon illustrates self-entanglement.
The simile of the waterwheel drawing from a well illustrates the cycle of birth and death.
The metaphors of illusions, mirages, and so forth illustrate the ignorance of the illusory nature that is free from "self" and "what belongs to self.
The phrase "arising from all that is unreal" means that names and signs give rise to various false imaginings; since the root of delusion is unreal, it arises as illusory appearances.

The manifestations of illusion are fundamentally empty; they are devoid of both the characteristic and that which is characterized, and neither arising, abiding, nor ceasing can be found. Thus, they ultimately resolve into one's own mind alone.

In truth, they are not produced by false causes such as an independent creator; yet the ignorant and foolish do not realize this, falsely grasping at external objects and drifting along with various names and appearances.
“Mahāmati! As for those marks:

that which is illuminated by visual consciousness is called form; that which is illuminated by the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental cognition is called sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena. These are called marks.”
Mahāmati!

Those who engage in conceptual construction (vikalpa) establish various names and manifest various characteristics; just as there are distinct names for elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, men, women, and so forth, this is called conceptual construction.

Mahāmati! As for right knowledge, neither names nor marks can be apprehended therein; it is like a passing guest. The various consciousnesses do not arise, and it is neither annihilated nor eternal. It does not fall into the stages of any externalists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding those "names" and "characteristics," the subsequent explanation of these two factors—name and characteristic—does not transcend the six consciousnesses, which grasp the six sense objects.
That which is named is the "name," and that which is grasped is the "characteristic. The manifestation and designation of various names and characteristics is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Names such as "elephant" or "horse" manifest their respective characteristics through these very names. Once both name and characteristic are established, one asserts that this thing is thus determined and not otherwise; this is called conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The three dharmas mentioned above pertain to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
From "Right Knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*) downward, the characteristics of awakening are clarified according to the dharma of the noble ones (*ārya*).

Regarding the statement that name and appearance (*nāma-rūpa*) are unattainable: this means that when seeking right knowledge, one simply awakens to the fact that names and appearances are unreal, like passing travelers; thus, the consciousness-mind does not arise, one departs from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and does not fall into the realms of ordinary beings or the Lesser Vehicle—this is Right Knowledge.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

By means of this right knowledge, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva neither establishes names and marks nor fails to establish names and marks; he abandons both the establishment and the denial of the two views, knowing that names and marks do not arise—this is called Suchness (tathatā)."
Mahāmati! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in suchness (*tathatā*), they attain the realm of non-existence and thereby reach the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

Having attained the Stage of Joy, they are forever separated from all external paths and evil destinies, and correctly abide in the supramundane destiny. With their realization of the characteristics of dharmas matured, they discern all phenomena as being like illusions and so forth. They personally realize the characteristics of the destiny of dharmas, depart from all deluded thoughts and views of strange and marvelous signs, and proceed through the stages in succession up to the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

In the interim, having fully blossomed his samādhis, powers, masteries, and supernormal faculties, and having attained the stage of a Tathāgata, he manifests various transformations through perfect illumination to mature sentient beings like the moon reflected in water. Having ultimately fulfilled the ten inexhaustible phrases, he expounds the Dharma with analytical distinctions for sentient beings of diverse inclinations and understandings.
"The Dharma-body is free from mental constructions; this is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into that which is attained through Suchness (*tathatā*).
This section precisely clarifies Suchness.
Because the aforementioned correct wisdom observes that names and characteristics are neither existent nor non-existent, it is said that "neither establishing nor not establishing" applies.

To abandon the two extremes of existence and non-existence, not to fall into the two slanders of diminution or augmentation, and for all names and signs to be non-arising—this is the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).
When a bodhisattva abides in suchness, they correctly demonstrate the characteristics of that which is attained through suchness.
Since it is called "suchness" (tathatā), how could there be anything attained?
It is by means of non-attainment that one attains; one attains the dharmas of cause and effect for both self and others.

What is termed the "realm of nothing whatsoever" is the departure from the marks of the two extremes of emptiness and existence; by this, one ascends to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), which is the first stage of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*).
Not departing yet departing, they depart from all external paths and evil destinies;
not abiding yet abiding, they abide in the supramundane right path;
without discrimination yet discriminating, they understand that all phenomena are entirely like illusions.
To realize without realization is to realize the path toward the Dharma of self-awakening.

This also involves departing from all deluded thoughts and views of the distinct characteristics of the nature; it is precisely the state where both the seer and the seen are abandoned, as described in the preceding text.

Proceeding in this sequence up to the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one attains various merits such as samādhis and powers; through these, one opens the Dharma up to the stage of the Tathāgata, manifesting physical forms everywhere for the sake of sentient beings, like the moon reflected in water.

Having fully perfected the ten inexhaustible vows, he expounds the Dharma according to the inclinations and understandings of others; his body is pure, transcending mind, thought, and consciousness—this is the mark of what is attained through suchness.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, how is it that the World-Honored One establishes the three natures as being included within the five dharmas? Or do they each have their own distinct characteristics and systems?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“The three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness are all subsumed within the five dharmas,
Mahāmati.”
Those names and characteristics are the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Mahāmati!

If, based on that false imagination, the mind and mental factors arise—arising simultaneously with names, like the sun and its light—distinguishing and maintaining various distinct characteristics, this is called the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
"Mahāmati! Correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are indestructible; therefore, they are called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Since the five dharmas have been clarified above, the meaning of the three natures is contained therein.

Now, because the preceding and succeeding sections have been subsumed, he asks again whether there are also individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and specific tenets (*svasiddhānta*) outside of those subsumptions.
In the response, the answer first addresses the general inclusion, which may be understood accordingly.
Next, regarding the specific allocation of dharmas and characteristics: first, "conceptualizing based on names and forms" refers to that from which [the conceptualization] arises.
"That conceptualization, in turn, belongs to dependent origination" is stated from the perspective of that which is produced.

If the mind and mental factors arise based on deluded thought, it is said that the mind-king and its mental associates arise based on discrimination; their arising is simultaneous, like the sun and its light, which are never separated from one another.
The conceptualization of various characteristics, each maintaining its own name without mutual confusion, is the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

Correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are both non-conditioned; therefore, they are indestructible and are called the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). These are the three natures as they enter into the five dharmas.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,

the eightfold discrimination of the false imagination manifested from one's own mind— namely, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the characteristics of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses— is an unreal characteristic, for it is a false imagination."
When the two graspings of "self" and "what belongs to self" are extinguished, the two forms of non-self arise.

Therefore, Mahāmati, these five dharmas constitute the sequential continuity of the stages of the noble wisdom of self-realization for Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas; all Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within them.
This clarifies that the five dharmas are subsumed within the eight consciousnesses.
Based on the manifestations of one's own mind, eight kinds of discrimination arise; these are all false and unreal characteristics.

If one can abandon the two kinds of self-grasping, then both the grasper and the grasped will cease; from this, the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness arises, which is precisely right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*).
Thus, although consciousness and its objects differ, they all converge within the five dharmas and possess no distinct intrinsic characteristics;
this is the clear intent of our thesis. Furthermore, these five dharmas encompass the three vehicles, the Buddhas, and all phenomena whatsoever.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, the five dharmas are:
appearance, name, conceptualization, suchness, and right knowledge.
Mahāmati!"
Regarding "sign" (*nimitta*): when a location, shape, color, image, or the like appears, this is called a sign.
When something possesses such a sign and is designated as a "vase" or the like—being precisely that and nothing else—this is called a "name" (*nāman*).
To establish various names and manifest various characteristics—such as "jar" and so forth—is what is called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding mind and mental factors.
Those names and those characteristics are ultimately unobtainable; from beginning to end, they are without awareness.
The absence of mutual succession among all phenomena and the departure from unreal conceptualization is called *tathatā* (suchness).

Since the ultimate self-nature is truly determined and unattainable, that is the characteristic of suchness; it is the point of entry into which I and all Buddhas conform and enter. For the sake of all sentient beings, we expound it according to reality, establish it, and reveal it. Entering into perfect awakening therein, one is neither annihilated nor eternal, and conceptualization does not arise. This conformity with the noble realm of self-realized wisdom—a characteristic unattainable by any outsiders, *śrāvakas*, or *pratyekabuddhas*—is called right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
Mahāmati! These are called the five dharmas.
The three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness—all the Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within them.
"Therefore, Mahāmati!
You should personally cultivate skillful means and also teach others; do not follow after others.
This section restates the names and explains their meanings through yet another approach; while they are largely the same, there are slight differences, each for its own specific reason.
The characteristic comes first and the name follows; they do not deviate from the reality of the name, as each has its own sequence of priority.
As for the difference between the other two [aspects], the former is based on one's own practice; therefore, wisdom comes first and suchness follows.
This includes both transforming others and, by reversing their sequence, refers to what is called "the place where I and all Buddhas accord with and enter," which is Suchness (*tathatā*).
"Universally expounding for the sake of sentient beings according to reality" and so forth refers to Right Wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).
Thus, one should know that this passage encompasses both transforming oneself and transforming others.
Here, "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the distinct shapes of the perceived objects, such as forms and so forth.
"Names" (nāman) refers to the designations, such as "vase," established in dependence upon those various characteristics.
Because of these names and signs, there arise various objects of attachment for the mind and mental factors; this is called delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

To thoroughly realize that names and signs ultimately do not exist, but are merely the successive discriminations of a deluded mind—to observe in this way and be free from all delusive conceptualizations—is called Suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding "truth, certainty, and so forth," this again refers to the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*), indicating the point of entry for all Buddhas. Based on their own self-realization, they expound it according to reality; being neither annihilated nor eternal, it cannot be attained by those who are ordinary, limited, biased, or heterodox, and is therefore called "correct wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "all Buddha-dharmas enter therein," this is a general conclusion concerning the four types [of precepts] based on the principle of mutual inclusion; thus, it differs from what was stated above.
As for the precept stating "to learn for oneself and teach others" and further saying "do not follow others," this means one must not be led astray by names and appearances (*nāma-rūpa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The five dharmas, the three natures, And the eight kinds of consciousness,
The two kinds of selflessness— These fully encompass the Mahāyāna."
"Name, mark, and false discrimination, The two kinds of self-nature,
Correct wisdom, and suchness— These constitute the perfected nature.
Regarding "completely encompassing the Mahāyāna," this means that the four aforementioned dharmas universally encompass all teachings of the Great Vehicle.
Conversely, all Buddha-dharmas are also universally subsumed within these four dharmas.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
As the World-Honored One has stated: "The Buddhas of the past were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; those of the future and the present are likewise.
How is it that the World-Honored One accepts [this] as being spoken according to reality?
Is there further meaning?
I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately grant me liberation.

The Buddhas of the three periods of time are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; although this is frequently stated in the scriptures, does the number of these Buddhas correspond exactly to what has been described, such that one receives [the fruit] accordingly?
Is this because there is a distinct meaning?
Therefore, he requested further, as described at length.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It would be better to speak of their reception [of enlightenment]: the measure of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is not like that of the sands of the Ganges.

Why is this? Because they transcend worldly expectations and cannot be illustrated by worldly analogies; yet, because ordinary fools harbor notions of permanence and outsiders foster evil views through their delusions, leading them into an endless cycle of birth and death, I wish to cause them to weary of and detach from the wheel of saṃsāra, so that they may apply themselves with diligence and excel further. Therefore, for their sake, I say: 'The Buddhas are easy to see; they are not as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower.'"
"Therefore, he ceased his expedient seeking.
At other times, he again observed those to be converted and spoke thus: 'A Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower.'"
"The udumbara flower has never been seen before, is not seen now, and will not be seen in the future.

Yet the Tathāgata is seen by all in the world; it is not because he establishes himself through his own power that it is said, 'The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is like the udumbara flower.'"

"Mahāmati! That which is established by itself and validated by itself transcends worldly expectations; it cannot be believed in by those ordinary, foolish people. It is the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, for which no analogy can be found. It is the true Tathāgata, who has transcended the characteristics perceived by the mind, intellect, and consciousness, and thus cannot be illustrated by any analogy."
"Mahāmati!
However, when I speak of a metaphor comparing Buddhas to the sands of the Ganges, there is no fault.
In the reply, he first points out the error.

For the number of all Buddhas exceeds the sands of the Ganges and surpasses the scope of what can be conceived by the worldly mind; thus they cannot be adequately illustrated by any metaphor—how could it be merely by the sands of the Ganges?

In general, when metaphors are established, their meanings are not uniform. For those who are ordinary and ignorant and have not yet received transformation, birth and death are endless; therefore, the Buddha teaches them that the Buddhas are easy to encounter, unlike the *tāpa* flower, so as to prevent them from conceiving thoughts of despondency and to cause them to cease their futile pursuit through expedient means. By urging them to advance toward the Buddha-way, he uses the difficult to manifest the easy, and thereby encourages their progress.

Sometimes, having observed those who have received transformation, he speaks to them of the rarity of encountering a Buddha, which is like the udumbara flower, so as to cause them to admire and aspire toward the Path; this is how he urges them on.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the *tamdava* flower is difficult to see, it is not said that it has never been seen, nor that it will not be seen now or in the future; rather, since the Tathāgata is seen by all people in the world, we know that those who say the Tathāgata is like the *tamdava* flower merely intend to evoke in others the realization that he is truly difficult to encounter.

However, these two metaphors—whereby what is difficult to express is made easy—are merely matters concerning the Buddha’s transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-prayoga*), not the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.
Therefore, it is said: "One does not establish [the truth] through one's own conventional understanding."

If one discusses self-realization, it is peerless in the world and beyond the reach of analogies; all ordinary and ignorant people are unable to believe and accept it, nor can it be known or seen by mind, intellect, or consciousness.
Nevertheless, there are times when one establishes [teachings] for the sake of transforming others; what fault could there be in this? "Mahāmati!
It is like the sands of the Ganges: though all kinds of fish, turtles, crocodiles, lions, elephants, horses, humans, and beasts may trample upon them, the sand does not think: "
"Those beings disturb me," thus giving rise to false conceptualization; yet his self-nature is pure and free from all defilements.

The Ganges River of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s own realized noble wisdom is like the sands of great power, supernatural faculties, and mastery; though all outsiders, humans, and beasts may disturb him, the Tathāgata does not harbor thoughts of them nor give rise to false conceptualization.
The Tathāgata is tranquil and free from discursive thought.

Because the Tathāgata’s original vow is to bring peace to sentient beings through the bliss of samādhi, he is without affliction or disturbance; he is like the sands of the Ganges, without distinction, and because he has severed both greed and anger.

The insentient things of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, though trampled upon by fish, turtles, humans, beasts, and the like, do not give rise to thoughts of vexation or disturbance; this serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom and sovereign supernormal powers, which, even when subjected to the disturbances of non-Buddhists, humans, and beasts, do not give rise to conceptual thoughts.
It is because, by the power of his original vow, he benefits and brings peace to sentient beings without any discrimination of love or hatred.
*Śūcimukha* is translated as "Fish that Kills its Young.

It is like this: just as the nature of the earth is like the sands of the Ganges, when the kalpa ends and all the earth is consumed by fire, that element of earth does not abandon its own nature, for it arises simultaneously with the element of fire.
Furthermore, foolish commoners conceive the notion that the earth is being burned, yet the earth is not burned because it has fire as its cause.
In this same way, Mahāmati,
the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is indestructible, like the sands of the Ganges.
This statement that the nature of the sand does not change is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body being eternally abiding.
Regarding the statement that this is the self-nature of the earth, there is both the phenomenal (the event) and the noumenal (the principle).
In terms of the phenomenal, they share the same quality of solidity; therefore, they are either sand or stone.
According to principle, it shares the same true nature as solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion.
Therefore, when the kalpa ends in conflagration, the nature of earth remains as it was; for both earth and the fire element are equally manifestations of arising.
Fools do not know or see this, and thus they say, "It is burned.
As for the cause of fire: because earth lacks fire it is not burned, and because fire lacks earth it does not continue; therefore, earth cannot be burned.
The same is true for the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, which neither transmigrates nor changes. "Mahāmati!

Just as the sands of the Ganges are without limit, so too is the radiance of the Tathāgata; it is likewise without limit, universally illuminating all the great assemblies of Buddhas in order to bring sentient beings to maturity."
"Mahāmati!
It is like the sands of the Ganges: if one seeks a sand grain distinct from the others, it can never be found.
In the same way, Mahāmati!"
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has neither birth-and-death nor arising-and-ceasing, because the causes and conditions [for them] have been severed.
This section states that "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" and "without limit" serves as a metaphor for the immeasurable radiance of the Tathāgata, which universally illumines all things.

The statement "no different from sand" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s transcendence of the two kinds of birth and death—segmented and transformative—because all causes and conditions, both out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*), have been severed.
“Mahāmati! For example, it is impossible to perceive any increase or decrease in the sands of the Ganges.
In the same way, Mahāmati!”
The Tathāgata’s wisdom brings sentient beings to maturity without increase or decrease, for it is not a physical phenomenon (*rūpadharma*).
Physical phenomena are subject to destruction, but the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is not a physical phenomenon.

This metaphor illustrates how the Tathāgata, through the wisdom of skillful means, brings sentient beings to maturity, yet there is neither increase nor decrease in the Dharma-body, unlike the form-body which undergoes birth and extinction.
The "body-dharma" refers to the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
"Just as when pressing the sands of the Ganges, oil cannot be obtained;

even so, although all these beings in extreme suffering oppress the Tathāgata, he does not abandon the *dharmadhātu* until those beings have attained *nirvāṇa*, due to his own aspiration for samādhi and his great compassion."

"Dust and sand contain no oil; this is a metaphor for how the Tathāgata, though oppressed by the manifold sufferings of sentient beings until the very last of the wriggling creatures has entered nirvāṇa, cannot relinquish his profound resolve and aspiration, because he fully accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings through his great compassion."
“Mahāmati! It is like the sands of the Ganges, which flow along with the water; they do not exist without the water.
In the same way, Mahāmati!”
All dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata flow toward nirvāṇa; therefore, it is said that they are like the sands of the Ganges.
The Tathāgata does not follow the flow of the various migrations, for "migration" (gati) signifies destruction.
Mahāmati!
The original limit of birth and death is unknowable; because it is unknowable, how can one speak of "going"?
Mahāmati!
"Going" has the meaning of cessation, yet the foolish do not understand it.
When the sands of the Ganges flow along with the current, the ignorant see only the flowing sand and do not see the water; yet when observed with wisdom, it is not that there is no water.

This metaphor illustrates that all dharmas taught by the Tathāgata accord with nirvāṇa; just as there is "following the current" without the sense of "going," it is said that "the Tathāgata does not flow along with the currents of various goings."

This means that by awakening to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one does not follow after appearances; therefore, this is not the same as "going" (*gati*), for "going" carries the meaning of the destruction and cessation of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Regarding the "original limit of birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra-pūrvakoṭi*) and so forth, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"The original limit of birth-and-death cannot be known; since it cannot be known, how can one speak of a destination?"
"Mahāmati!
The movement toward meaning is cessation, yet ordinary fools do not know it.
"Movement" (gati) means "going" (yāti).
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
if the original limit of birth and death for sentient beings cannot be known, how can liberation be known?”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"When the causes—the beginningless habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of false discrimination (*vikalpa*) and the faults of deception—are extinguished, one realizes that external objects are but manifestations of one's own mind; thus, the body of false discrimination is transformed, yet liberation is not annihilation."
Therefore, "boundlessness" does not mean that nothing exists at all; rather, it is an alternative designation for that which is conceptualized by false imagination.

When one observes both the internal and external, free from false imagination, there is no separate sentient being; wisdom (*jñāna*) and its objects (*jñeya*), as well as all phenomena, are entirely quiescent.
"Because one does not recognize that false imaginings are manifestations of one's own mind, false imaginings arise; if one recognizes this, they cease.
Since the fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of saṃsāra and liberation are equal in principle, why is one knowable and the other unknowable?

In the response, it is stated that beginningless falsehood and so forth are precisely the cause of liberation; to know external objects as manifestations of one's own mind, whereby the body of false imagination is transformed, is itself liberation.
Since the transformation of deluded thoughts is itself liberation, it is truly not extinguished.
Because it is not extinguished, it pervades all places; therefore, it is called "boundless.
Since its essence is boundless, it is said that "it is not entirely nothingness."

Regarding those false conceptualizations and so forth, it is said that the locus where those false conceptualizations are transformed is designated by such names as "liberation" and "the infinite. Because the essence of the transformation does not itself transform, these are called different names for the same thing.

Regarding the observation of the internal and external: previously, by means of the self-mind manifesting the knowledge of external objects, one realizes that the external lacks any external characteristics. Returning to this principle to illuminate the internal mind, one finds that the internal and external are of one suchness (*tathatā*). Departing from delusive appearances, there is only true suchness, with no other dharmas whatsoever; therefore, it is said that "there are no distinct sentient beings."
Wisdom (*jñāna*) and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are realized as being without mutual dependence; therefore, all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely quiescent.

To clarify that those who do not recognize what is manifested by their own mind are bound again, it is explained that these deluded thoughts of arising and ceasing exist solely through the recognition or non-recognition of one's own mind and consciousness. If one recognizes one's own mind, there is no delusion that will not be extinguished.
However, as for those who speak of consciousness yet fail to extinguish delusion, it is because they have not attained true consciousness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Observe the various Teachers, Who are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Neither destroyed nor departing, Nor yet reaching a final end— This is what constitutes equality;
Thus one observes all Tathāgatas.
Like the sands of the Ganges, They are entirely free from all faults.
"Flowing with the stream yet its nature is eternal—this is the Buddha’s perfect awakening.
"Unchanging" praises the fact that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding;
"not departing" praises the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma as not following along with the various streams of transmigration.
Furthermore, regarding that which is not ultimate: if one observes the Tathāgata as being indestructible and non-departing, it is not yet ultimate.
One should observe that all Buddhas are like the sands of the Ganges—equal and without distinction, free from all faults and afflictions.
Furthermore, as for the statement that "the nature of following the stream is eternal," this means to follow the stream toward ultimate *nirvāṇa*; this is true eternity and perfect enlightenment.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I only pray that you will explain the characteristic of the momentary disintegration of all phenomena.
World-Honored One,
in what sense are all phenomena momentary?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"All dharmas refer to the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate; the conditioned and the unconditioned; the mundane and the supramundane; the faulty and the faultless; the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing; and that which is grasped and that which is not grasped."
A *kṣaṇa* is the shortest duration of time and the most minute unit of thought.
As it is said: "In the time it takes a strong man to snap his fingers, there are sixty-one *kṣaṇas*."
Therefore, the incessant arising and ceasing of mental thoughts is defined as a *kṣaṇa*.
Furthermore, the impermanence and disintegration of phenomena is also a *kṣaṇa*; these are all the characteristics of the deluded consciousness of sentient beings.

The preceding section discussed the transformation of the body of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), explaining that the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are impermanent; therefore, this [section] raises the question regarding the characteristic of the momentary disintegration (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) of all phenomena.
In the response, the names of all phenomena are first enumerated, and they are subsequently explained.

“Mahāmati! Briefly stated, the mind (citta), the intellect (manas), the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), and their habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are the causes of the five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandha). These—the mind, the intellect, the mental consciousness, and their habitual tendencies—nurture the wholesome and unwholesome conceptualizations of the ignorant and foolish.”
The "brief explanation" is stated in contrast to the detailed explanation that follows.
Mind, consciousness, and habitual tendencies are the causes of birth and death; the five aggregates are the effects of birth and death.

Because one does not understand that mind, consciousness, and habit-energies are mutually nourishing, there arise the momentary, out-flowing delusions of the three realms and the six classes of ordinary beings.
"Wholesome and unwholesome" refers to the three wholesome and three unwholesome [paths of action].
"Mahāmati! Cultivating the bliss of samādhi, the correct reception of samādhi, and dwelling in happiness in the present life is called the noble, wholesome, and untainted (anāsrava).
The cultivation of samādhi and so forth constitutes the cause and fruit of the untainted."
Samādhi is the cause;
dwelling in the joy of the Dharma is the fruit.
These untainted dharmas of the noble ones of the three vehicles are untainted, and being untainted, they transcend momentary thought.
“Mahāmati! As for the wholesome and the unwholesome, they refer to the eight consciousnesses.
What are these eight?
That which is called the Tathāgatagarbha is named the Ālayavijñāna;

it consists of the mind (citta), the intellect (manas), the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), and the five bodies of sensory consciousness (pañca-vijñāna-kāya). This is not what is taught by the non-Buddhists, Mahāmati!

The five groups of consciousness are conjoined with mind (*citta*), mentation (*manas*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); they possess the characteristics of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, undergo successive transformation and disintegration, and flow on in a continuous stream.
They arise as an indestructible body, arising and ceasing moment by moment.
Failing to realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind, they cease in succession as other consciousnesses arise with various distinctions of form and appearance.

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the five sensory consciousnesses arise together in mutual correspondence; because they do not abide for even a single moment, this is called a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*).

Below the section on "wholesome and unwholesome," the characteristics of the momentary (*kṣaṇika*) and non-momentary are explained in detail. Although these names appear again, their meaning is presented comprehensively.

As for the statement that the *tathāgatagarbha* is called the "consciousness-store" (*vijñānagarbha*), this refers to the eighth consciousness; since the names and characteristics of this consciousness, extending even to the five sensory consciousnesses, emerge from the authentic teachings, it is said: "This is not what is taught by the non-Buddhists."
The phrase "the five groups of consciousness" precisely clarifies their momentary characteristics.

Regarding the statement that "mind, intellect, and consciousness arise together," this means that the aforementioned five consciousnesses—eye and so forth—simultaneously apprehend objects along with mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). These possess the characteristics of being wholesome or unwholesome, arising either in immediate succession or in an intermingled manner; hence it is said that they "undergo successive transformation and disintegration while flowing in a continuous stream."

The interval between the sense faculties and their objects has never been interrupted; "not destroyed" means not severed. "The body arises" refers to the arising of the five groups of consciousness. Since that which arises must perish, it is said to be "both arising and ceasing."

Because one fails to realize that all objects are manifestations of one's own mind and becomes attached to their differentiated forms and appearances, which arise and perish from moment to moment, it is said: "One consciousness perishes in succession as another arises."

Regarding the "appropriation of the mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*): when the five sense organs grasp the five objects, consciousness returns to the mental consciousness; it is from this that good and evil arise. Furthermore, because the mental consciousness simultaneously apprehends its objects and gives rise to discrimination, it is called "arising in conjunction" (*saṃprayukta*).

Regarding "not abiding for even a single kṣaṇa": this means that the arising and ceasing of all consciousnesses is incessant; they do not remain here nor there, and there is not even a moment's rest. This is the characteristic of a kṣaṇa.

“Mahāmati! ‘Moment’ (kṣaṇa) refers to the ālayavijñāna, the tathāgatagarbha, and the momentary habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of the co-nascent consciousnesses together with the manas. The untainted habitual tendencies are not momentary; they are not perceived by ordinary, ignorant people.”

"Because they are attached to the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇavāda*), they do not realize that all phenomena are neither momentary nor non-momentary; thus, through their nihilistic view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), they destroy unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
The section beginning with "As for 'momentary'" below serves to reiterate what precedes and introduce what follows.

Although these two types of characteristics both generally arise based on the various consciousnesses, their respective sources differ; hence it is said that "it is called the storehouse-consciousness," and so forth.

Thus, those consciousnesses that arise from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of [defiled] consciousness are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), whereas those that arise from untainted habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*) are non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*).

If it is already untainted (*anāsrava*) yet is still termed "habitual energy" (*vāsanā*), this means that its substance is the seventh consciousness; because the grasping of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) still persists, although it is not momentary, it has not yet attained ultimate, true, and permanent untaintedness. It is, rather, the realm of the noble ones (*ārya*) of the three vehicles, and thus is not perceived by ordinary, ignorant people.
Ordinary fools conceive of creation and advocate a theory of momentariness; not only do they fail to realize that things are non-momentary, they are unaware even that they themselves are momentary.

As for those with the view of annihilation—referring to the ascetic practices of worldly non-Buddhists who falsely grasp at nirvana—they fall into the view of annihilation rather than attaining untainted nirvana; therefore, it is said that they "destroy unconditioned dharmas."
“Mahāmati! The seven consciousnesses do not undergo transmigration; they do not experience suffering or pleasure, and they are not the cause of nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!”

The Tathāgatagarbha experiences pleasure and pain, co-arising with their causes, whether being born or ceasing; intoxicated by the four stages of dwelling and the stage of ignorance, the deluded and ignorant are unaware of it, as momentary views and false imaginings permeate the mind.

Regarding "the seven consciousnesses do not undergo transmigration," this follows upon the preceding discussion of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state and distinguishes [these] from the six and eight consciousnesses.

This is because the consciousnesses of these two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), having already severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), no longer transmigrate within the three realms and do not undergo the suffering or pleasure of birth and death; thus, they differ from the six consciousnesses.
Because it is not the cause of *nirvāṇa*, it differs from the eight consciousnesses; for it is the eight consciousnesses that receive perfuming and can thus become the cause of *nirvāṇa*.

As for the *tathāgatagarbha*, this term correctly refers to the eight consciousnesses, as they are able to contain and store both good and evil, and follow conditions to flow through the cycle of birth and death, as well as the causes and effects of suffering and pleasure.
The four stages of abiding (catur-vihāra-bhūmi) refer to the branch and derivative ignorance (avidyā).
The stage of abiding of ignorance (avidyā-vāsabhūmi) refers to the fundamental ignorance.
Due to being intoxicated by this ignorance, one undergoes two kinds of birth and death.
The deluded thoughts of ordinary fools permeate their minds, such that they cannot understand this and give rise to the view of momentariness.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Just as gold, diamond, and the relics of the Buddha possess extraordinary qualities and are never subject to decay."
Mahāmati!

If there were moments within the attainment of the uninterrupted [state], then the noble ones would not be noble; yet the noble have never ceased to be noble. They are like gold or a diamond, which do not perish even after being weighed throughout the course of kalpas.
"Why do ordinary, foolish people, being unskilled in my teachings of hidden intent (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*), conceive the notion of momentariness regarding all internal and external phenomena?

When the Tathāgata originally answered the question concerning moments, he stated that a moment involves destruction; yet, when he spoke directly of that which is indestructible, it was because that which is deluded is momentary, while that which is awakened is not momentary.

It is like diamond and the like; among metals, diamond is the most refined essence. Because it has been smelted a hundred times, the ore and matrix are entirely consumed until only the pure essence remains, which no object can destroy—this is its extraordinary characteristic in the world.

Furthermore, it is like the Buddha’s relics: having been refined through the cultivation of the ten thousand practices, all defilements have been completely exhausted, leaving only the singular, pure, and true essence that nothing can destroy; this is the extraordinary characteristic of that which transcends the world.
The true permanence attained by the Tathāgata is likewise so; therefore it is said, "If one attains the uninterrupted [state], there would be moments," and so forth.
The Buddha means: how could there be moments in the true permanence realized by me through the *asaṃskṛta-samādhi* (unconditioned samādhi)?

Regarding the statement that "the sage may not be a sage": since there is no principle by which a sage has ever failed to be a sage, one knows that once awakened, there is no delusion; it is evident that this state is without even a single moment of lapse.
Therefore it is said: "Though the diamond be weighed throughout kalpas, it does not diminish.
Why is it that ordinary, ignorant people do not understand this secret teaching and instead conceive of all phenomena as being momentary?
"Concealment" means secrecy.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"As the World-Honored One has said, 'By fulfilling the six pāramitās, one attains perfect enlightenment.
What are these six?
That which arises and perishes in a single kṣaṇa refers to the affairs of this shore of birth and death.
That which is true, eternal, and indestructible is the principle of Nirvana, the further shore.
Thus, to travel from this shore to that shore, and to proceed from the momentary toward ultimate eternity—this is surely the merit of the Six Perfections!
It was for this reason that Mahāmati inquired further.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"There are three kinds of distinctions regarding the pāramitās: namely, the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane."
Mahāmati!

As for the worldly pāramitās, they are characterized by attachment to the notions of "self" and "what belongs to the self," and by grasping at the two extremes. For the sake of various places of rebirth and out of delight in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, one fulfills the dāna-pāramitā.
The same applies to morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the supernatural powers of ordinary beings and birth in the Brahma heavens.
In the response, it is stated that there are three types of the six perfections.

First, regarding the mundane six perfections, the phrase "clinging to and being attached to 'I' and 'mine'" refers to four faults in the practice of ordinary beings: [the fault of self-grasping, the fault of grasping at possessions, the fault of conceptual attachment, and the fault of false discrimination].
First, to calculate in terms of "self" and "what belongs to self" means one lacks the thought of delivering sentient beings;
second, to be attached to the two extremes means one cannot reach the other shore of the Middle Way;
third, to seek superior rewards means one cannot escape birth and death.
To be attached to the six sense objects is not the practice of giving without abiding; this is the fourth [point].

That non-Buddhists attain the five supernatural powers and are reborn in the Brahma Heaven is likewise achieved by cultivating the field of merit and practicing the six perfections of the untainted (anāsrava) path.

“Mahāmati! As for the supramundane pāramitās, because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into the grasping of nirvāṇa, they practice the six pāramitās while delighting in their own personal nirvāṇic bliss.”

This is what is practiced by those of the Two Vehicles; although they rely upon the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination to practice these six perfections, it is said that they "fall into the grasping for nirvana. Because they act solely for their own liberation and delight in the bliss of true emptiness, their practice differs from that of the Bodhisattvas.

"Regarding the supramundane, most excellent *pāramitā*: because one realizes that the measure of false discrimination is the manifestation of one's own mind, and because one understands the duality of one's own mind, one does not give rise to false discrimination. Not grasping at the various realms of existence as being real, and not being attached to the forms and appearances of one's own mind, one generates the *dāna-pāramitā* for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, thereby initiating the most excellent skillful means."
The precept that prevents the arising of false conceptualization regarding those very objects is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
That same non-arising of false conceptualization, which involves the patient acceptance of knowing the grasped and the grasper, is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
To apply diligent effort during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, and to practice in accordance with skillful means so that deluded thoughts do not arise—this is the *vīryapāramitā*.
To utterly extinguish all deluded thoughts and yet not fall into the grasping for the nirvana of the śrāvakas—this is the *dhyānapāramitā*.

The false imaginings of one's own mind lack intrinsic nature; when observed with wisdom, one does not fall into the two extremes. Thus, the previous body is transformed into something superior and indestructible, attaining the noble path of self-realization—this is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"This is what is practiced by the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching].
'Inclusion' refers to the six sense organs including the six sense objects.
'The two of one's own mind' refers to the duality of the means of treatment and the object of treatment, namely, practicing the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) to remedy stinginess and greed."

Once a Mahāyāna bodhisattva has realized that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone—meaning they practice giving without dwelling on form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects—then the duality of the "tamer" and the "tamed" is non-dual.
Because duality is non-dual, the three wheels are empty in essence; hence it is said, "do not give rise to delusive conceptualization.
That which gives is emptiness;
that which does not grasp is the emptiness of the recipient.
Without being attached to the marks of form, the object given is empty.
When a bodhisattva practices giving in this manner, it is for the sake of benefiting and bringing joy to all sentient beings; therefore, it is called the "supreme skillful means."

Regarding those very conditions and so forth, it means that by means of a mind well-cultivated in the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), one does not give rise to false conceptualization even toward conditions such as the observance of precepts; to maintain each and every thing in accordance with its true nature (*dharmatā*) is what constitutes morality (*śīla*).
To maintain the precepts in this manner is neither maintaining nor violating them;
to practice patience in this manner is neither opposing nor conforming;
to exert diligence in this manner is neither advancing nor being indolent.
To practice dhyāna in this manner is to be neither fixed nor distracted;
to practice prajñā in this manner is to be neither ignorant nor wise.

Naturally neither adhering to the two extremes nor departing from them, one abides in the Middle Way and proceeds directly to the other shore; this is the characteristic of the supreme-to-supreme pāramitā.

Regarding the statement within the perfection of patience that one "knows the grasper and the grasped," this means that the intrinsic nature of both the subject (grasper) and the object (grasped) is empty.
Regarding the two mentions of "skillful means" (*upāya*) within the perfection of diligence: the first refers to its specific characteristics, such as reciting scriptures;
the second refers to its general characteristic, meaning that diligence must be applied to all five perfections concurrently.

Regarding the statement in the *Dhyānapāramitā* that one does not fall into the category of the Śrāvaka, this means that while the Śrāvaka’s meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*) is predominantly excessive and they are attached to Nirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva is not like this.

Furthermore, regarding the six perfections, some say that delusive thoughts do not arise, some say they are entirely extinguished, and others say they have no inherent nature; thus, although the six perfections differ, they all take the departure from delusion as their foundation.
If one can depart from delusion, what practice could not be accomplished!

That the preceding body becomes increasingly superior and indestructible refers to the progressive advancement of the six perfections up to Prajñā; the resulting body of wisdom (jñānakāya) is superior to the previous five and cannot be destroyed. To attain the noble state of self-awakening is, moreover, the ultimate realization of Prajñā.
Thus, although these three categories encompass the middle and lower levels, their intent truly lies in the highest of the high; let those who practice choose accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Emptiness, impermanence, and momentariness— These are constructed by the deluded imaginings of fools."
Like a river, a lamp, or a seed, one should conceive of them as momentary.
The cessation of the turbulence of moments is tranquility, free from activity;
that all phenomena are non-arising—this, I call the meaning of "momentariness."

The Tathāgata constantly uses metaphors such as a flowing river, a seed, and a lamp to dismantle those false imaginings regarding conditioned phenomena, demonstrating that they are all empty, impermanent, and momentary.
Ordinary, deluded people do not understand this hidden teaching and give rise to momentary conceptualizations.

The phrase "the cessation of momentary turbulence" and so forth correctly explains the meaning of the aforementioned concealment; that is to say, if one can comprehend the moment, one can cease turbulence and realize quiescence, thereby naturally becoming free from conditioned activity. Thus, all phenomena are unborn, which is why the meaning of the "moment" (kṣaṇa) is taught.
"When things arise, they are subject to cessation; this is not taught for the sake of the foolish.
The nature of uninterrupted continuity is perfumed by false conceptualization;
ignorance is its cause, and from it the mind arises."
"Until form has yet arisen, what divisions exist in the interim?
When things arise, they necessarily perish; this is indeed the constant principle of arising and ceasing.
To speak thus for the sake of the ignorant would only proliferate names and signs; therefore, one refutes the dharma of arising and ceasing.

First, the characteristic of arising is shown as that which is to be refuted; namely, the nature of uninterrupted continuity, which is the arising and ceasing of each moment. Because it is perfumed by false conceptualization and has ignorance as its cause, the deluded mind of each moment arises from that [ignorance].

Next, within the section clarifying the refutation [of the opponent's position], the first part refutes the characteristic of arising. The passage beginning with "even when form has not yet arisen," etc.,承接 (continues from) the previous point: although the mind has already arisen, at the time when form has not yet arisen, there is in the interim no portion of its own basis; thus, this mind does not arise because it lacks form.
Regarding the phrase "what portion," the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* reads "where does it abide"?
"When the preceding [moment] has ceased in succession, and another mind arises following it,
if it does not abide at the time of the form, how could it arise with that as its object?"
"Because it arises from that, it does not arise from a cause as it truly is.
How can there be nothing established, yet one know that there is momentary destruction?
