This clarifies the characteristic of the cessation of the continuum: although form has already arisen, the mental continuum ceases; thus, form and mind do not depend upon one another.
Even if there are other minds that arise following those forms, if the mind does not abide in form, upon what could it depend to arise?
This is because, moment by moment, it neither abides nor grasps.

Although this mind possesses form, it likewise lacks the nature of arising; for if it were to arise from that [form], then it would itself lack any obtainable nature of arising. Therefore, it is said: "It does not arise from causes as they truly are."

Next, regarding the characteristic of destruction: since even the characteristic of momentary formation cannot be found when sought through the aforementioned analysis, how much less could there be the characteristic of momentary destruction?
"Destruction" (*bhaṅga*) is synonymous with "destruction" (*nirodha*).
Once birth and cessation have been destroyed, one returns to the original, true permanence.
"The practitioner’s meditative absorption, the diamond, the Buddha’s relics,
and the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven— these are the imperishable things in the world."
Abiding in the attainment of the True Dharma, the Tathāgata is fully endowed with wisdom;
the bhikṣu attains equanimity—how then could one perceive moments?
Like a gandharva-city or a magical illusion, form has no such thing as a moment.
"Regarding unreal forms and so forth, one views them as if they were real.
This verse concerns the four dharmas that are not subject to destruction:
namely, the first is the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the practitioner; [the others follow].
The vajra is the second;
the relics of the Buddha are the third;
and the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven are the fourth—this heaven is not destroyed by the three calamities and serves as the beginning of formation for subsequent kalpas.

This celestial being and the vajra are indestructible things of the mundane world; meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*) and the relics (*śarīra*) of the Buddha are indestructible things of the supramundane world.

Next, to demonstrate the person capable of attaining indestructibility, it says: "Those who abide in and attain the True Dharma. This means that while the Tathāgata is fully adorned with right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), the bhikṣu [is adorned] with equanimous meditative equipoise; both attain [this state] by means of the True Dharma.
However, although diamond and the Ābhāsvara heaven are said to be indestructible, they are nonetheless impermanent.

As for "how one perceives the momentary," this is a concluding refutation of the preceding [position]: if one does not perceive the momentary as described above, by what principle would one perceive the momentary?
Therefore, the city of Gandhavatī is used as a metaphor for this.

Indeed, illusory forms are not inherently momentary; yet sentient beings, within the midst of false phenomena, reckon them to be substantially existent. This is just like viewing the illusory forms of Gandhavatī as real—how could they be anything other than non-momentary?
"If one realizes the momentariness [of all things], delusion is itself the ultimate reality.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The World-Honored One has prophesied that Arhats shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, being no different from the Bodhisattvas.
Since the dharmas of all sentient beings do not enter nirvāṇa, who then reaches the Buddha-way?
From the time he first attained Buddhahood until his parinirvāṇa, did he not utter a single word during that interval, nor offer any response?
Since the Tathāgata is eternally in samādhi, does he neither reflect nor discern?
If emanated Buddhas perform the deeds of a Buddha, for what reason do they speak of the mark of the momentary, successive destruction of consciousness?
Why are Vajrapāṇi and his retinue constantly present to guard them?
Why do they not establish the limit of the beginning (pūrvakoṭi)?

The Māra manifested and his demonic deeds appeared; the retribution for evil karma was revealed through the cases of the Māṇava Candra and the woman Sundarī, as well as by emerging with an empty bowl. Since these obstacles of evil karma were manifest, how could the Tathāgata have attained all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) while not being free from such faults?
This passage contains seven questions:
first, the question regarding the bestowing of predictions upon the śrāvakas;
second, from "from all the assemblies" down to "there was no answer," the question as to why the Buddha said he does not preach the Dharma.
3. Regarding the Tathāgata’s constant descent, the question asks why he waits for contemplation before preaching the Dharma;
4. Regarding the emanated Buddha’s descent, the question asks about the teaching on the characteristic of momentary disintegration;
5. The question asks for what reason there are Vajra-attendants.
Sixth, he asked about the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*); seventh, he asked about the nine afflictions (*navasaṃkleśa*).

As for these nine afflictions: they are the rising of the celestial Māra’s army; the Brāhmaṇī Ciñcā tying a wooden bowl to her belly; the killing of the woman Sundarī; entering the village of Vairaṇā to beg for alms and returning with an empty bowl; eating horse fodder; suffering pain in both the head and back; being wounded in the foot by a thorn; the laying of a fire pit; and poisoned rice. These constitute the nine.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
“So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“I have spoken thus for the sake of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, and to encourage and advance those who practice as bodhisattvas. This and other worlds contain those practicing as bodhisattvas who take pleasure in the *nirvāṇa* of the Śrāvaka vehicle; [I speak thus] in order to cause them to leave the Śrāvaka vehicle and advance toward the Mahāyāna.”
The transformation Buddha bestows predictions upon the śrāvakas; it is not the Dharma-body Buddha.
Mahāmati! For this reason, the predictions given to the śrāvakas are no different from those given to the bodhisattvas.
Mahāmati!

As for "non-differentiation," it means that for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all tathāgatas, there is a single flavor of liberation through the severance of the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa), but not through the severance of the cognitive hindrances (jñeyāvaraṇa).
Mahāmati! As for the obstacle of knowledge, it is purified by the superior realization of the selflessness of phenomena;
as for the obstacle of afflictions, it is severed by first practicing the realization of the selflessness of persons.
"The seven consciousnesses cease, the dharmic hindrances are liberated, and the habitual tendencies of the ālayavijñāna are extinguished;
this is ultimate purity. This answers the first question.

Regarding the statement "it is for the sake of *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) that it is taught," etc.: because the bonds of both cause and fruit are exhausted, it is called "without remainder"; however, it is not the ultimate state. Although they are granted a prediction [of enlightenment], they must still practice the bodhisattva path; this is merely an inducement to advance those of the Hīnayāna.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "In this world and other worlds," it is said that there are bodhisattvas who have initially cultivated the great practice but then take pleasure in minor fruits; for their sake, the Buddha bestows predictions of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) to urge them forward, and thus it says, "progressing toward the Mahāyāna."
This refers to the meaning of the predictions for śrāvakas given in this sutra.

The bestowal of predictions upon śrāvakas occurs precisely in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; however, these are currently provisional predictions made by a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha), which is why it says, "this is not [the prediction] of the Dharma-Buddha."

The statement that they are not different from Bodhisattvas refers merely to the fact that they equally sever the obstacles of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and attain the single flavor of liberation; it does not mean that they have severed the obstacles to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

If the obstacles to knowledge were severed, one would perceive the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and attain the sublime, pure realm of the Tathāgata, which is not the case for Śrāvakas.

Śrāvakas merely sever the afflictions of views and thoughts and perceive the selflessness of persons; they have not yet destroyed ignorance or perceived the selflessness of phenomena, and for this reason they differ from Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "the seven consciousnesses are extinguished," this is discussed in terms of whether the two obstacles have been abandoned or not by means of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses. The two vehicles merely extinguish the seven consciousnesses but have not yet abandoned the obstacle of dharmas; as it is said, "merely being free from delusion is called liberation."
If phenomena such as hindrances are extinguished, only then is there ultimate purity; thus, one knows that identity and difference are not easily discussed lightly.
"Because of the primordially abiding dharma, prior and posterior are not its nature."
This answers the second question.

It means that because the primordially abiding dharma (dharmatā) neither increases nor decreases, there was no path of the Buddha to be attained before, no nirvāṇa to be entered after, and no dharma to be spoken of in between; therefore, it is said that "before and after are not its nature."
"Non-nature" means being free from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Because his original vows are inexhaustible, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma without deliberation or investigation; because he is transformed by right wisdom and his mindfulness is never false, he is without deliberation or investigation.
Because the habit-energies of the four stages of abiding and the stage of ignorance are severed, the two afflictions are eliminated, and one is freed from the two kinds of death.
One awakens to the selflessness of persons and phenomena, and the two obstructions are severed.
This answers the third question.
The Tathāgata’s vow to deliver sentient beings is inexhaustible; he responds without deliberation and speaks without speaking. Therefore, it is said: "without thought or examination."

This is because one who has thoroughly investigated and exhausted correct wisdom perfectly mirrors the Dharma-realm; like an image appearing in a mirror, what need is there to wait for deliberation before preaching the Dharma?
Furthermore, it says "the four stages of abiding" (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) and so forth, which refers to the ultimate exhaustion of the fruits [of afflictions].

That which is to be severed are the two obstacles; that which is to be abandoned are the two deaths; and that which is to be realized is the dharma-gate of non-dual self—how could these be the deeds of a transformation Buddha? "Mahāmati!

The mind, the intellect, the mental consciousness, and the seven [consciousnesses] such as the visual consciousness are the causes of momentary habitual tendencies; they are excluded from the category of the wholesome and the outflow-free, and thus no longer undergo cyclic existence. Mahāmati!
"The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and of suffering and happiness; it cannot be realized by foolish ordinary people whose minds are distracted by emptiness.
This answers the fourth question.
The names "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), and so forth refer to the seven bodies of consciousness; these are, in fact, the single sixth consciousness, the *vastu-vijñāna*.
As for the distinction between that which perishes moment by moment and that which does not, this difference arises merely from the perspective from which it is described.

If one considers the various consciousnesses from the perspective of their momentary habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they are subject to destruction; however, from the perspective of the category of wholesome and outflow-free states (*anāsrava*), they are not destroyed. Because their nature is detached and non-momentary, they no longer undergo cyclic existence; this is precisely the meaning of being indestructible.
However, the momentary habitual tendencies (*kṣaṇika-vāsanā*) belong to the category of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*).
Those of the wholesome and outflow-free category (*anāsrava-kuśala-pakṣa*) belong to the category of the seventh consciousness (*saptavijñāna*).
This is the explanation of the meaning of "perishing" and "not perishing" through the contrast between the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses].

If we consider the seventh and eighth consciousnesses in relation to one another, the seventh consciousness clings to a self; because its perceptions and mental activities have not yet been forgotten, it is subject to destruction. Only the eighth consciousness is indestructible; therefore, when specifically mentioning the seven consciousnesses beginning with visual consciousness, the intention is to imply the eighth consciousness, which remains indestructible.

The Tathāgatagarbha specifically reveals the ālayavijñāna; that is to say, when this consciousness is in saṃsāra it is called saṃsāra, and when it is in nirvāṇa it is called nirvāṇa. It provides [beings] with suffering and pleasure, yet it is not as yet pure. Thus, it is neither identical nor separate, neither destroyed nor indestructible; therefore, it cannot be realized by ordinary, ignorant people.
Regarding "disturbed by emptiness": those of the Lesser Vehicle who are attached to emptiness are thus disturbed by emptiness. "Mahāmati!
He whom the Vajrapāṇi protectors follow and guard is merely a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha), not the true Tathāgata."
Mahāmati!

A true Tathāgata is free from all faculties and measures; all the faculties and measures of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists are extinguished. Having attained the bliss of the present dharma and dwelling in the patience regarding the knowledge of the uninterrupted dharma, he is therefore not protected by the Vajrapāṇi.

All transformation buddhas are not born of karma; these transformation buddhas are neither buddhas nor separate from buddhas. They preach the Dharma by means of signs created by sentient beings, such as a potter’s wheel, rather than speaking of the realm of self-realization from their own state of direct penetration.
This answers the fifth question.
Within the question, there are two modes of discourse: the general discussion (*prasaṅga*) and the specific discussion (*vibhaṅga*).
Regarding the general discussion, since the Buddha possesses both true and emanated forms, it is said that the one protected by the Mallas is an emanated Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Being free from all faculties, measures, and so forth, it is said that the true Buddha does not fall into the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases of self or others. Because he has attained the bliss of the present dharma and dwells in the patience of the knowledge of the uninterrupted dharma, he ultimately abides in wisdom and abandonment; since his merit-dharmakāya is always conjoined with meditative concentration, there is no need for protection.
Regarding the separate discussion: although these are emanations (*nirmāṇa*), they likewise do not require protection. This is due to two reasons:

first, "emanation" refers to a manifested appearance, which is a responsive adaptation; furthermore, that which suddenly arises from non-existence is called an emanation. Both of these appear in response to the capacities of sentient beings and differ from the birth of ordinary beings through actual karma, which necessitates protection—this is the first reason.

Second, it is said that an "emanation Buddha" is neither distinct from the Buddha nor separate from him; rather, the emanation arises from the Truth (*tathatā*). Thus, being neither identical nor different, it likewise does not require protection—this is the second reason.

However, the function of transformation must depend upon sentient beings; since sentient beings engage in action, they require the assembly of various conditions (*pratyaya*). Therefore, the Buddha also preaches the Dharma through the assembly of conditions. Thus, when it is said, "based on the discourse of the potter," and so forth, it precisely takes up the meaning of the assembly of conditions.
This is indeed protection through non-protection, like that of the Vajrapāṇi; how could this not be a transformation?
As for "not being within the sphere of self-communication," it differs from the True Buddha, who speaks only of the realm of self-realization.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
foolish people give rise to the view of annihilation based on the cessation of the seven groups of consciousness;
because they do not realize the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), they give rise to the view of permanence."
"Because of one's own deluded imaginings, one does not know the primordial limit;
because the wisdom of one's own deluded imaginings is extinguished, one attains liberation.
This answers the sixth question.

The primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi) is not something that cannot be designated; however, because sentient beings have been unable to emerge from the realm of their own deluded imaginings (vikalpa), they remain ignorant of this primordial limit.

To the utmost extent of their imaginings, they do not transcend the two views of annihilationism and eternalism; therefore, it is said: "Fools [speak of] the cessation of the sevenfold body of consciousness," and so forth.
Based on what they know, because they perceive nothing beyond the seven consciousnesses, they give rise to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

Yet, failing to realize that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is inexhaustible, and seeing its moments of thought as a continuous succession, they give rise to the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
Because one's own deluded thoughts reach inward but not outward, one is unable to know [the truth]; it must wait for these deluded thoughts to be extinguished before liberation occurs.
Regarding the "extinguishing by wisdom," this indicates that delusion does not extinguish itself, but must be extinguished through wisdom.
"Because the habit-energies of the four abodes and the abode of ignorance have been severed, all faults are severed.
This answers the seventh question.

Since the Tathāgata has exhausted both the primary afflictions and their residual habits across the five abodes and has forever forgotten the two types of death, how could there ever again be matters such as the activities of Māra?
Nevertheless, all of these are merely expedient manifestations for the sake of sentient beings.
These seven questions and seven answers, according to the divisions in the sutra, may be divided into ten sections or categorized into six; readers should examine this in detail for themselves.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The three vehicles are also not vehicles; The Tathāgata does not perish.
That which all Buddhas have prophesied Is said to be free from all faults and evils."

For the sake of those with uninterrupted wisdom and for the sake of nirvana without remainder, the Buddhas employ expedient means to entice and advance those of inferior capacity; therefore, they speak by way of concealment.
The wisdom arising from all Buddhas is precisely that which discriminates and explains the Path.
The various vehicles are not truly vehicles; they are not nirvana.
Desire, form, existence, and views—these are said to be the four stages of abiding.
They arise from the mental consciousness; consciousness is the house and the mind is that which dwells therein.
"The mind, eye-consciousness, and so forth, are taught as impermanent through their cessation;
yet for those who hold views of nirvāṇa, they are taught to be eternally abiding.
"Non-vehicle" means that which is not the Buddha-vehicle.
That which is indestructible refers to the true Buddha.
Because he is not a vehicle, he is granted the prediction of the One Vehicle;
because he is the true Buddha, it is said that he is free from all faults and evils.
The first and last of these two responses in this verse also concurrently include the fifth question and response.
For the sake of those with uninterrupted wisdom (*ānantarya-jñāna*) and others, the initial response is restated; the intended meaning can thus be understood.

Regarding "the wisdom arising from all Buddhas," this verse answers the second question. It refers to the wisdom attained from the initial arising [of the path] at the Bodhi tree; subsequently, the path is explained through differentiation. This is to manifest "non-explanation" by means of explanation, rather than saying there is no explanation. Because it is described in terms of non-nature, the Three Vehicles are not the Buddha Vehicle, and the emptiness of true reality (*tathatā-śūnyatā*) and *nirvāṇa* are not the ultimate *nirvāṇa*; thus, it is said that they are "not explained."
"Desire, form, existence, and views," etc., refers to the four abodes (*catur-vāsa-bhūmi*); that is to say, the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms are divided into these four abodes.

"The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)" and below answers the sixth question: it means that the mind arises from the eight consciousnesses, and since the eight consciousnesses are what the mind dwells within, they are called its "abode."
Speaking from this perspective, it is inherently impossible to give rise to the view of annihilation based on the cessation of the sevenfold consciousness-body.

Furthermore, those who speak of impermanence regarding the cessation of the mind and the visual consciousness, or who conceive of these as nirvana, do so because they are ordinary people or non-Buddhists with their own deluded views; they do not know the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). It is for their sake that the Tathāgata teaches [the nature of] permanence.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva asked in verse:
“Those bodhisattvas who are resolved to seek the Buddha-way—
how should they consume alcohol, meat, and onions?”
I pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One, out of compassion, will explain for me:
how can that which fools greedily cling to— which is foul, impure, and without reputation,
and which even tigers and wolves delight to consume— be fit for eating?
"Eating gives rise to all manner of faults; not eating is a source of merit and goodness.
I pray that you will explain to me the transgressions and blessings of eating and abstaining.
While the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma within the palace of the King of Ghosts, the various yakṣas thought that mealtime was approaching, for they do not eat unless there is meat.
Because Mahāmati wished to cause the various spirits to give rise to a mind of compassion, he requested the Tathāgata to explain the merits and faults of eating meat and abstaining from eating meat.
After Mahāmati Bodhisattva had spoken these verses as a question, he further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us the virtues and transgressions of eating and not eating meat."

I and all the bodhisattvas shall, in the present and the future, preach the Dharma for the sake of various beings who hope to eat meat, causing those beings to direct their hearts toward one another with loving-kindness.
Having attained the mind of loving-kindness, each will clearly understand their respective stages of abiding and swiftly attain ultimate, unsurpassed bodhi.
Having brought their own stages to rest, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas shall likewise swiftly achieve unsurpassed bodhi.

Even among the various non-Buddhist practitioners who follow evil and heterodox doctrines—those with false views who are inverted by clinging to the extremes of nihilism and eternalism—they still maintain prohibitions against eating meat; how much more so for the Tathāgata, who is the protector of the world and has perfected the True Dharma, would he eat meat?
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"Even for the various non-Buddhists, such as the Lokāyatas, who give rise to views of existence and non-existence and cling to the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, there are prohibitions that do not permit the eating of meat; how much less could the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, who nurtures all with great compassion and is the refuge of the world, ever permit both oneself and others to eat meat?"
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
“Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat; however, I shall now briefly explain them for you.

That is to say, all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, been related to one another through successive causes and conditions and have constantly been one’s own kin. Because they are regarded as kin, one should not eat meat.”
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been revolving incessantly in birth and death; there has never been one who has not been their father, mother, brother, son, daughter, or relative, nor even a friend, loved one, or servant. Having changed births to receive the bodies of birds, beasts, and so forth, how can one take them and eat them?"
"Because the flesh of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, oxen, horses, humans, beasts, and so forth is sold mixed together by butchers, one should not eat meat.
Because it grows from impure elements and vapors, one should not eat meat."

When sentient beings smell the odor [of meat], they all give rise to terror, just as dogs, upon seeing outcasts such as Caṇḍālas or Taṃbas, loathe them and bark in a pack out of fear; therefore, one should not eat meat.
"Vani-candāla" is translated here as "butcher.
"Tambava" is translated here as "one who eats dog meat," and also refers to a hunter.
Furthermore, because it prevents the arising of a compassionate mind in practitioners, one should not eat meat.
Because it is that which the foolish and ignorant crave—foul, putrid, and impure—and because it lacks a good reputation, one should not eat meat.
Because it causes various incantations and rituals to fail, one should not eat meat.
Because those who kill living beings perceive the form and give rise to consciousness, becoming deeply attached to its flavor, one should not eat meat.
Furthermore, because those who eat meat are abandoned by the devas, one should not eat meat.
Because it causes the breath to become foul, one should not eat meat.
Because it results in many evil dreams, one should not eat meat.
Because tigers and wolves will smell its scent in secluded forests, one should not eat meat.
Because it causes one to lose moderation in eating and drinking, one should not eat meat.
Because it prevents practitioners from developing a sense of weary detachment (*saṃvega*), one should not eat meat.
I have previously said: "In all that you consume as food and drink, you should regard it as the flesh of your own child or as taking medicine; therefore, you should not eat meat."
"There is no such basis for permitting the eating of meat.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhasūtaputra who ate various kinds of meat until he eventually came to eat human flesh. His ministers and subjects could no longer endure this, so they plotted a rebellion and cut off his stipend."
Because those who eat meat have such faults as these, one should not eat meat.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
whenever there are killers who slaughter and trade living beings for the sake of profit, those foolish sentient beings who eat meat use money as a net to capture that meat.

Those who take life, whether by means of wealth or by means of hooks and nets, capture those beings that move through the air, water, or on land, killing them in various ways and slaughtering or selling them for profit.
Mahāmati! Furthermore, there is no fish or meat that exists without being taught [as such], sought after, or conceptualized.
For this reason, one should not eat meat.
Mahāmati!

At times I have spoken of prohibiting five kinds of meat, or restricted ten kinds; however, in this sutra, through skillful means, I now permit no exceptions at any time or in any manner, and thus all [meat-eating] is entirely forbidden.
Mahāmati!
Even the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have no food to consume, much less fish or meat;
nor do they instruct others to eat them.
Because they are preceded by great compassion, they regard all sentient beings as if they were their only child; therefore, one should not allow them to eat the flesh of their children.
The passage states that there are no fish or meats that are not taught, sought after, or thought of [to be killed]; this should be understood in two senses:
first, that those who slaughter and sell do not merely kill for themselves, but also instruct others to kill—this constitutes "teaching."
To capture those sentient beings with hooks, nets, and the like for the sake of wealth and profit is *vitarka* (seeking);
to perceive their forms, give rise to consciousness, and develop attachment through the body is *saṃjñā* (perception).

Next, it is said that although sentient beings who consume meat out of ignorance do not kill themselves, by eating meat they promote the trade of slaughter, which carries the meaning of "teaching to kill";
using money as a net to capture various meats carries the meaning of "seeking";
and the meaning of "conception" is the same as above.

However, among the Five Constant Virtues of the Confucians, benevolence (*ren*) is primary. As it is said: "One may fish with a hook but not with a net; one may shoot with an arrow but not at birds roosting.
"One does not kill the fetus, nor does one destroy the young."
"The gentleman keeps his distance from the kitchen," it is said;
these are all manifestations of benevolence (*ren*), yet they do not prohibit the eating of meat.

Our Buddha, however, takes the non-killing of sentient beings as the foremost precept, regarding even the smallest insects and crawling creatures no differently than his own children. He taught that if one does not observe this precept, one severs the seed of compassion (*karuṇā*); how vast, then, is the scope of his benevolence!
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"All have once been our kinsmen; They are base, filthy, and mixed with impurities.
Born and grown from what is unclean, Their very scent strikes terror into one's heart."
All meats and onions, as well as various leeks, garlic, and the like,
along with all kinds of intoxicating liquors— those who practice the path should always keep far from these.
They should also always avoid sesame oil and beds with perforated frames.
"Because those tiny insects within it cause extreme terror. Regarding the phrase "free from sesame oil":

according to the customs of foreign lands, it is the rule to pound sesame until worms are produced and then press them; as they yield much juice and increase the fat content, how could such things be fit for consumption?
The various forms of cavities are often swarming with insects; one must not sit or lie there, for the insects will become terrified at the time of sitting or lying down.
"Food gives rise to heedlessness; Heedlessness gives rise to discursive thoughts;
From discursive thoughts, craving arises. Therefore, one should not eat."
From food arises craving; craving causes the mind to become deluded and intoxicated.
This intoxication increases desire, and one is not liberated from birth and death.
To profit, they kill sentient beings; with wealth as a net, they ensnare various meats.
Both are evil karmas; upon death, one falls into the Hell of Wailing.
If there is no thought of being taught or sought [for oneself], then there are no three kinds of pure meat.
That [meat] does not exist without a cause; therefore, one should not eat it.
Because of this, all those practitioners will be utterly shunned;
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, will all reprove them.
By preying upon one another, they shall fall after death into the species of tigers and wolves.
Foul-smelling and loathsome, they are born ever deluded.
They are mostly born as caṇḍālas, hunters, or tāmras;
or they are born as dhīvanīs, as well as those of a meat-eating nature.
"Rākṣasas, cats, wildcats, and the like, / Are born everywhere within this [world].
/ The *Gajabandhana*, the *Mahāmegha*, / And the *Aṅgulimālīya*,"
Tāyini means "rākṣasī" in this language.
Baddhasimha, Mahāmegha, and Aṅgulimāla are all titles of sūtras.
"And with this Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, I have completely prohibited the eating of meat."
Reproached by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas,
those who eat meat without shame or remorse will remain in constant ignorance and darkness throughout every birth.
Having first declared the prohibitions regarding what is seen, heard, or suspected, all meat has already been renounced.
Due to deluded thoughts and lack of awakening, one is born in places where meat is consumed.
Just as the fault of lustful desire obstructs the noble liberation,
so too do wine, meat, scallions, leeks, and garlic all serve as obstacles to the Noble Path.
Sentient beings in future ages, out of ignorance regarding meat, will say:
"This is pure and without fault; the Buddha permitted us to eat it.
One should regard eating it as taking medicine, and likewise as eating the flesh of one's own child.
Contentment gives rise to disenchantment; practicing the way, one goes for alms.

For those who dwell securely in a mind of loving-kindness, I say they are always disenchanted [with worldly things], such that even tigers, wolves, and other evil beasts may constantly dwell and roam alongside them.
If one eats various kinds of flesh and blood, all sentient beings will be terrified;
therefore, practitioners should cultivate a heart of loving-kindness and not eat meat.
One who eats meat lacks compassion and wisdom, and forever turns their back on true liberation.
Furthermore, it contradicts the marks of a noble being; therefore, one should not eat it.
One will be born into the lineage of Brahmins, or into various places of spiritual practice, or into families of wisdom and prosperity—this is due to abstaining from meat.
As the Buddha’s discourse on the "Chapter on the Mind" drew to a close, Mahāmati again requested that he provide instructions regarding wine, meat, and other such matters to conclude it.

This is because our Buddha established his transformation through teaching with the equality of the single nature as its foundation, with compassion as the same essence as one's own body as its core intent, and with leading others into the Way as its primary principle; thus, nothing takes precedence over purity and the avoidance of transgressions. Furthermore, since his purpose was to rescue beings and deliver sentient life, nothing is more supreme than the law of cause and effect regarding sin and merit.

Therefore, following the main body of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it thoroughly elucidates the four kinds of clear admonitions and the three stages of gradual progress; its warnings in this regard are even more earnest, and thus it may also be regarded as a text for the purpose of circulation.
The text first requests a general admonition, followed by a specific admonition.
In the Buddha’s response, seventeen reasons for why one should not eat meat are fully enumerated, and so forth.

Next, regarding the demonstration of the general and specific scope of prohibitions, it first states that in the provisional teachings of the Small Vehicle, five types [of meat] may be permitted: namely, those seen, heard, suspected, killed for oneself, and so on.
As for the remaining [animals], it seems appropriate that eating them should be permitted, or perhaps ten specific types are prohibited— namely humans, snakes, elephants, and so forth—
but other classes are not mentioned, suggesting they should generally be allowed.
Nevertheless, I speak with particular caution, stating only that [the practice] is for the purpose of restraint; there has never been a word of approval.
Even if there were a temporary expedient, it would still be a matter of necessity.
Furthermore, it is said that this sutra opens up the provisional means and severs [the practice of meat-eating] entirely; its words may indeed be called profound and piercing.
Yet, commentators still regard the prohibition against eating meat as a point of doubt and difficulty.

It seems that some commentators have stated: "This sutra says that bodhisattvas should not eat meat; therefore, we know that [the permission to eat meat] still remains open within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings. Consequently, they conclude that this sutra merely prohibits bodhisattvas [from eating meat].
As for the fact that the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings are still preserved and permitted [in this scripture], some claim it is an error of the compiler.

I maintain that this is not so; rather, it is precisely because the *Laṅkāvatāra* is said to follow after the four *Āgamas* that it preserves the doctrine of gradual teaching (*anupūrvika-yāna*), which differs from the sudden prohibitions of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. This serves to show that the section of this scripture belongs to the Vaipulya (Extensive) class, and nothing more than that.
What you call "surviving" is merely its literary expression; how can you say that the substance still survives? Furthermore, do you consider this to be an error?
If not, the Sūtra says, "All are completely severed. What does this statement mean?

Alas! When great precautions have been established and strict regulations have been formulated, people in the world still occasionally transgress them; how much more so when no such warnings are provided!

This allows us to see the profound depth of karmic habituation. There are even those who no longer praise the holy life (brahmacarya) themselves and cause others to enter into non-discipline (aśīla); I know that such persons bring this calamity upon themselves.

However, this sutra states that all phenomena are merely manifestations of one's own mind; if one truly understands that good and evil are but the mind, how could one follow after deluded thoughts while contravening the holy teachings?
Be cautious; exert yourself.

This concludes the fourth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-ratna*. This scripture consists of four fascicles and four chapters, collectively titled "The Heart of the Buddha’s Words," and does not have individual titles for each chapter.
The Wei edition consists of ten fascicles divided into eighteen chapters (*pinda*).
The Tang edition consists of seven fascicles divided into ten chapters.

Later, the śramaṇa Baochen of the Eastern Capital annotated the Tang edition by inserting the remaining eight chapters of the Wei edition in their proper sequence, thereby also forming eighteen chapters.
Now, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* is the teaching on the nature of mind expounded by all Buddhas.

When the Buddha taught this Dharma, he caused all bodhisattvas to enter their own mental realms; thus, the title "The Chapter on the Mind of the Buddha's Words" (*Buddhaghoṣa-citta-parivarta*) is given according to the general purport of the entire scripture.
As for the separate division of chapters in the Wei and Tang editions, these were divided according to the structural sections of the sūtra so that students might easily understand them.
Although the text contains both general and specific categories, the underlying principle remains one and the same.
Formerly, when the Yao Qin court commissioned a monk to lecture on this sutra, he did not divide it into sections and his exposition lacked logical order. Consequently, the ruler remarked:
"In our Buddha’s sutras, every dialogue between teacher and disciple has its beginning and conclusion; how can this monk’s lecture on the sutra alone lack such order?"
At that time, Dao’an was in Luoyang; hearing this report, he sighed and said, "Why must we all suffer such humiliation?
From then on, regardless of whether a sutra was large or small, they followed the precedent of dividing it into three parts.

Later, when Vasubandhu’s commentary was transmitted to China, it indeed accorded with his [Huiyuan’s] assertions; that is to say, the division of the sutra as formulated by Vasubandhu is perfectly consistent.

Today, the four-fascicle version still preserves the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Heart-Word" (*Buddhaguhya-hṛdaya-varga*). Following the listings found in the Wei and Tang editions, these chapter titles have been placed at the beginning of each section to prevent those who lecture and study from becoming confused regarding the structural divisions.
However, among the eighteen chapters, only the *Dhāraṇī* and *Gāthā* chapters are missing.
Furthermore, the text of the first chapter, the "Chapter on Exhortation," is incomplete; it contains only six lines of verse, which serve as a separate introductory section.
The prohibition against eating meat constitutes the *prasaṅga* (concluding) section.
Thus we know that while the text is abbreviated, its meaning is not.
I, the monk Ruxi, respectfully record this.

Postscript to the Newly Carved *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: Since His Majesty ascended the throne and assumed the precious calendar, he has extensively propagated the Confucian classics while also incorporating the Buddha-vehicle to transform and civilize the world.

Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, along with the *Vajracchedikā* and *Laṅkāvatāra*—these two sūtras—are used to elucidate the study of the mind; they are truly the sun and moon for those lost on the path and the vessel for crossing the sea of suffering.

Then, in the tenth month of winter in the tenth year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued for the Zen Master of Tianjie, the subject Zongle, and the Dharma Master of Yanfu, the subject Ruyi, to provide a new commentary and explanation.

In the first month of the spring of the following year, my new commentaries on the *Heart Sūtra* and the *Diamond Sūtra* were completed; they were presented for the Master’s perusal and have already been published.

In the seventh month of autumn, the commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was again completed; the Emperor ascended to the Xihu Pavilion, where Zongle and Ruyi, along with other attendant ministers, presented it for his inspection.
Having read it, the Emperor was pleased and said:
"This commentary on the sutra is indeed precise; it may be circulated throughout the realm so that scholars may study and discuss it."
Zongle immediately complied with the imperial decree and carved the woodblocks at the Tianjie Chan Monastery in the capital.

When Ruyi returned to Hangzhou’s Yanfu Monastery, he privately reflected that since both he and Zongle had been granted the same imperial edict, it would be inappropriate to restrict the publication to Tianjie; rather, they should jointly publish this sutra at Yanfu.
However, as the volumes were so vast and extensive, he was unable to fulfill his ambition, and he worried about this day and night.
Thus, the Zen Master of Jingci, His Majesty’s Subject Yijian, composed a preface to exhort his fellow practitioners and those who delight in goodness to assist in its completion.

The work began in the fifth month of the summer of the following year and was completed in the eleventh month of winter; the total expenditure is said to have been five hundred and sixty-four strings of cash.

Now, this single scripture, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, fully encompasses the essential tenets of the four teachings—Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect. Thus, its refutation of the partiality of the Hīnayāna and its destruction of the delusions of false views are nothing other than the desire to manifest the self-awakened, correct wisdom of the Perfect School.
Furthermore, its phrasing is ancient and profound, making it exceptionally difficult for readers to comprehend.

The śramaṇa Baochen of the Eastern Capital once composed a commentary on it; although his citations and references appear comprehensive, they frequently fail to accord with the intent of the scripture.
Master Shu Tai Lei’an Shou inherited the discursive arguments of Baochen, yet he himself was unable to extend his own views by even a single peck of grain.
Both of these [masters] are devoid of merit.

Only Master Baiting Shan Yue, relying on the principles of the Tiantai teachings, composed the *Tongyi* (Comprehensive Meaning), which stands far apart and transcends ordinary ranks; yet even when verified against the explicit passages of the sutra text, it cannot avoid having its deficiencies—how much less can one hope for anything else!

Just as Zhiyi, through his vast, eloquent, and unimpeded wisdom, sported within the ocean-like treasury of Vairocana, there was no teaching of the Tiantai or Jiaxiang schools that he did not harmonize and subsume; thus, although his commentaries drew upon the records of the Baotang school, he repeatedly cross-referenced and verified them, striving never to deviate from the original intent of the Tathāgata’s sūtras.

Zongle was further able to discern the underlying purport and condense prolix expressions into essential and appropriate forms; he thus caused the obscure texts and profound meanings of several centuries to shine forth with clarity. Truly, he may be called one who spiritually inherited the Emperor’s gracious favor toward the common people and widely illuminated the methods established by the Great Awakened One for teaching and saving sentient beings!
Alas! The Great Dharma of the Buddha can only be promoted by emperors and transmitted by patriarchal masters.

Now that we have encountered such a magnificent occasion all at once, those who read this sutra may, on a small scale, contemplate the distance between evil and aspire to transform toward goodness; on a great scale, they may contemplate the enlightened mind and realize their true nature. In this way, they will not fail to repay the profound virtue of the Sage Emperor.
